note: Events that killed people in large numbers, used to say which years of which places are hard to find a death record for, and why. Black outlines on the History map. Every toll is a range from the sources, never one number; an event that is contested says so. Built by hand, then each entry filled and checked from Wikipedia, Wikidata and one further source (see scripts/validate-mortality in check-data.py). The area is a modern country outline, a circle or a box and shows where, not the borders of the day.

types.genocide: Genocide (as the cited sources describe it)
types.atrocity: Mass atrocity or system of killing

events.name: Plague of Justinian and the first plague pandemic

toll.text: Estimates for the whole first plague pandemic (541 to about 750) run from 15 million to 100 million deaths across the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East.
toll.note: Covers all recurrences, not only 541-549. No census exists; figures rest on chronicles. Wikidata lists both 15M and 100M.

events.says: Plague caused by Yersinia pestis reached Egypt in 541, spread through the Byzantine and Sasanian lands and the Mediterranean, and kept returning in waves until about 750.
events.open: Scale is disputed: a 2019 PNAS study (Mordechai and colleagues) argues the 'tens of millions' figures are not supported by wider evidence; Sarris and others criticise its method.

sources.title: The Justinianic Plague: An inconsequential pandemic? (PNAS 2019, abstract)

events.name: The Black Death

toll.text: Estimates for Europe run from about 25 to 50 million deaths (WHO says over 50 million); some put all of Eurasia at 75 to 200 million.
toll.note: No reliable counts; losses varied by place. A 1351 papal tally of Christian Europe gave 23.84 million. Wikidata lists 75M.

events.says: Plague pandemic that spread from Central Asia and the Black Sea to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East between 1346 and 1353, caused by Yersinia pestis.
events.open: No exact figures exist. The share of Europe's population lost is put from about 25% to 60%, and a 2022 pollen study found some regions little affected.

events.name: Italian plague of 1629–1631

toll.text: Figures range from at least 280,000 deaths to about one million in one summary, and about two million (30-35% of northern Italy) in an economic history study.
toll.note: Northern and central Italy. Milan about 60,000 and Venice about 46,000 are reported. Wikidata lists 1,000,000.

events.says: Plague spread through northern and central Italy from 1629, carried with troop movements of the Thirty Years' War, and hit Milan and Venice hard in 1630-1631.
events.open: Totals differ widely between the sources and the cited sources do not reconcile them; they also differ on whether to count northern Italy alone.

sources.title: Plague and long-term development (Alfani and Percoco, Economic History Review)

events.name: Great Plague of London

toll.text: Bills of Mortality recorded 68,596 plague deaths in London in 1665; Clarendon thought the true figure about double; summaries say about 100,000; a contemporary put England at about 200,000.
toll.note: Low is the recorded London count for 1665; high is a contemporary national estimate for 1665-66. Records undercount (the poor, Quakers).

events.says: Bubonic plague struck London from 1665 to 1666, killing a large share of its people, and spread to other English towns and villages such as Eyam.
events.open: Recorded burials undercount the dead, and the highest figure covers England as a whole, not London alone.

events.name: Great Plague of Marseille

toll.text: Over 100,000 deaths in Marseille and Provence in 1720-1722, about half in the city; one scholarly study gives as many as 126,000.
toll.note: City and surrounding Provence combined. City-only counts are less settled. Wikidata lists 100,000.

events.says: Plague arrived at Marseille by ship in 1720 and spread through Provence over the next two years, ending as the last major plague outbreak in Western Europe.
events.open: City-only deaths are uncertain, and the death rate across the wider area is put at 25% to 50% depending on district.

sources.title: The Great Plague Scare of 1720 (Cindy Ermus)

events.name: Smallpox epidemic in the Aztec lands

toll.text: Smallpox in Mexico in 1519-1520 is put at 5 to 8 million deaths; another framing gives one-quarter to one-half of central Mexico's people.
toll.note: First smallpox wave only, not later epidemics. Pre-contact population is itself uncertain. Wikidata has no death count.

events.says: Smallpox came with the Spanish expedition of 1520, reached Tenochtitlan that autumn, killed rulers and commoners, and weakened the Aztec capital before it fell.
events.open: Totals depend on uncertain pre-contact populations; the 40-50 million figure sometimes quoted is for the whole New World and is not a figure for this epidemic.

sources.title: Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico (Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4), 2002)

events.name: Cocoliztli epidemics of New Spain

toll.text: Estimates for the epidemic that began in 1545 run from 5 to 15 million deaths in New Spain; about 800,000 are reported for the Valley of Mexico alone.
toll.note: A CDC-published review gives 7-17 million for the 1545 and 1576 epidemics together. Wikidata lists 7M and 17M.

events.says: A fast hemorrhagic fever swept the Mexican highlands from 1545, killing great numbers of Indigenous people; a second large outbreak followed in 1576.
events.open: Cause is debated (Salmonella Paratyphi C versus a native viral hemorrhagic fever worsened by drought), and tolls rest on uncertain population estimates.

sources.title: Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico (Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4), 2002)

events.name: Epidemics and the depopulation of the Americas
events.wiki: Population history of Indigenous peoples of the Americas

toll.text: The sources give population estimates, not a death count: roughly 60.5 million people before 1492 and a loss of about 90% within a century, from epidemics along with violence and disruption.
toll.note: Pre-1492 estimates range from 8 to 112 million; deaths cannot be split by cause. Wikidata lists 2M and 100M, unlike the sources.

events.says: After 1492, Indigenous populations of the Americas fell sharply over the next century or more, through Old World epidemics, war, enslavement and upheaval.
events.open: How much was disease versus violence and forced labour is contested; some scholars (e.g. Stannard) call it genocide, others stress incidental disease. Baselines differ widely.

sources.title: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas
Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492 (Koch et al., Quaternary Science Reviews 2019)
sources.publisher: White Rose Research Online (University of Leeds)

events.name: First cholera pandemic

toll.text: The article says the total is unknown but millions died. For India it calls a reported 8.75 million an overestimate and cites a re-estimate of no more than one to two million.
toll.note: Regional counts only: Java over 100,000; Korea up to 100,000; Vietnam 206,835. About 10,000 British-service troops died.

events.says: Cholera spread from near Calcutta across South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East, East Africa and the Mediterranean coast between 1817 and 1824.
events.open: No overall toll exists, and the India estimates differ by several-fold. The numbering and dating of cholera pandemics also varies between historians.

events.name: Second cholera pandemic

toll.text: No overall total is given; the article describes hundreds of thousands of deaths in Europe, with local figures such as about 100,000 each in Russia and France and 6,536 in London.
toll.note: Wikipedia dates this pandemic 1826-1837; a journal article dates its European phase 1829-1849. Not a total for 1829-1851.

events.says: Cholera spread from India across Western Asia to Russia, Europe, Britain and the Americas, and east to China and Japan, reaching Britain in October 1831.
events.open: The dates are not agreed (1826-1837 versus 1829-1849 or later), and the sources give no overall toll, only national and city counts.

sources.title: The Second World Cholera Pandemic (1826-1849) in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (Journal of Community Health, 2015)

events.name: Third plague pandemic

toll.text: At least 15 million deaths worldwide between 1855 and 1960 are reported, including about 10-12 million in British India and 2.2 million in China.
toll.note: A floor ('at least 15 million'), not a point estimate. Wikidata has no death count.

events.says: Plague began in Yunnan, China, in 1855, spread by trade and shipping to all inhabited continents, and was considered active by the WHO until 1960.
events.open: The total is a minimum. The Manchurian pneumonic plague of 1910-11 (45,000-60,000 deaths) is counted in by some historians though it was epidemiologically distinct.

sources.title: Prolonged drought and associated social unrest on the Tibetan Plateau played a role in the emergence and spread of the Third Plague Pandemic (Communications Earth & Environment, 2026)

events.name: The 1918 influenza pandemic

toll.text: Estimates run from about 17 million (a 2018 reassessment) through at least 50 million (CDC) to figures above 100 million; about 500 million were infected. Covers 1918-1920, worldwide.
toll.note: Few countries kept reliable death records; India alone is put at 12-17 million, the US at 500,000-850,000 (CDC: 675,000).

events.says: Influenza A (H1N1) pandemic that spread worldwide in several waves from spring 1918 to 1920, infecting about a third of humanity, with notably high mortality among young adults.
events.open: The global toll is uncertain by a factor of six, and the 17 million figure is itself contested. The name 'Spanish flu' is misleading: the place where it began is unknown.

sources.title: 1918 Pandemic Influenza: Historic Timeline
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

events.name: The HIV/AIDS pandemic

toll.text: At least 42.3 million deaths from 1981 to 2024 (Wikipedia); WHO's July 2026 fact sheet says 44.2 million to date. The two differ mainly by cut-off year; deaths continue, about 570,000 in 2025.
toll.note: Cumulative HIV-related deaths since AIDS was recognised in 1981; the epidemic is ongoing, so the total keeps rising.

events.says: Disease caused by the retrovirus HIV, which passed from primates to humans in west-central Africa in the early to mid 20th century and was recognised as AIDS in 1981; it spread worldwide and continues.
events.open: Cumulative totals depend on the cut-off year and on modelled estimates, since death registration is incomplete in many countries. Wikidata lists earlier cumulative totals of 32 and 40.4 million.

events.name: Ebola epidemic in West Africa

toll.text: Between 11,308 and 11,328 deaths among about 28,600 reported cases, depending on source and cut-off: CDC 11,308, WHO about 11,325, Wikipedia 11,310 and 11,323, Wikidata 11,328.
toll.note: Reported cases only (confirmed, probable, suspected); WHO says the outbreak was substantially undercounted, so unreported deaths are not included.

events.says: Largest Ebola outbreak on record, centred on Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone from December 2013, with smaller outbreaks and imported cases elsewhere; declared over in June 2016.
events.open: The reported count is acknowledged to be an undercount; one 2014 study put unreported cases at 17-70%. The start is dated to December 2013 (first case) or March 2014 (first report).

sources.title: History of Ebola Outbreaks
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

events.name: The COVID-19 pandemic

toll.text: As of 18 Sept 2026, 7.1 million confirmed deaths; modelled excess-death estimates run from 18.5 to 35.2 million. WHO put excess deaths in 2020-21 alone at 14.9 million (range 13.3-16.6).
toll.note: The confirmed count is a floor of officially reported deaths and still moves; excess-death figures include indirect deaths and depend on models.

events.says: Global pandemic of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first detected in Wuhan, China, in December 2019; WHO assessed it as a pandemic on 11 March 2020 and ended the health emergency in May 2023.
events.open: Official counts are widely held to undercount. Excess-death estimates differ by method and source, and the share caused directly by the virus is debated. The end date depends on the definition used.

sources.title: 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021

events.name: Great Famine of 1315–1317

toll.text: No total count is given. The article reports 10-25% of the population of many towns died, about 10% in northern France and 10-15% in southern England; a Princeton historian says up to 10% in many regions.
toll.note: Only percentage losses for particular places exist, so no Europe-wide number of deaths can be stated.

events.says: Heavy rain from spring 1315 caused repeated harvest failures across northern Europe, from the British Isles and northern France to Germany and western Poland, with food shortages and mass death until about 1317-1322.
events.open: Historians debate the toll. Dates are given as 1315-1317 or 1315-1322, and the share lost is put at up to 10% of regional populations by one source and 10-25% for many towns by another.

sources.title: Medievalist Jordan 'really likes archives' (Princeton Weekly Bulletin, 31 March 1997)

events.name: Great Famine of 1695–1697

toll.text: About 150,000 died in Finland (25-33% of the population per a 1979 study) and 70,000-100,000 in Estonia and Livonia (about a fifth); no counts are given for Sweden or Norway. Covers 1695-1697.
toll.note: Low is the Finland figure alone; high adds the upper Estonia-Livonia figure. Sweden and Norway were also hit but have no counts, so are not included.

events.says: Cold, wet years in the 1690s ruined harvests in Finland, Estonia, Livonia, Sweden and Norway, and starvation and epidemic disease followed, worst in Finland and northern Sweden in 1696-1697.
events.open: The 150,000 figure traces to an 1899 work by Zacharias Topelius, not a modern demographic study, and the share lost varies by author. The Sweden and Norway tolls are unquantified.

sources.title: Great Historical Events That Were Significantly Affected by the Weather: 4, The Great Famines in Finland and Estonia, 1695-97
sources.publisher: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

events.name: Bengal famine of 1770

toll.text: Traditional estimates are 7-10 million (a quarter to a third of the population); some scholars call these exaggerated and say at least 1 million, and one revision gives about 1.2 million.
toll.note: No census existed. Company officials estimated about a third dead in 1770; W. W. Hunter later gave 10 million. Modern scholars call that inflated.

events.says: Famine in Bengal and Bihar after the monsoon failed in 1768-69, made worse by East India Company tax and grain policies and followed by smallpox and depopulation, worst in north Bengal and Bihar.
events.open: Reliable demographic data are lacking, so the toll is unsettled: 7-10 million is the older figure, 1.2 million a revision, and Dyson calls 10 million barely credible without offering a number.

sources.title: Fables of Famine: Bengal, 1770 and 1943 (ORIAS Summer Institute 2014, Parama Roy)

events.name: The Great Irish Famine

toll.text: The most accepted figure is about 1 million excess deaths in 1845-1852; other estimates range from half a million to 1.5 million (Cousens 800,000; Mokyr 1.1-1.5 million). Disease killed more than starvation.
toll.note: No civil death registration existed. The 1851 census counted about 422,000 deaths in a decade but its authors said it was incomplete.

events.says: Famine in Ireland after repeated potato blight failure, 1845-1852, worst in 1847, causing about a million deaths and over a million emigrants; the population fell by a fifth to a quarter by 1871.
events.open: The toll is an informed estimate. The label is contested: the article records that most historians reject calling the British response a genocide, while some scholars and campaigners argue it was one.

events.name: Northern Chinese famine of 1876–1879

toll.text: 9.5 to 13 million deaths, including about 5.5 million in Shanxi, 2.5 million in Zhili, 1 million in Henan and 0.5 million in Shandong; the University of California Press says at least ten million. Covers 1876-1879.
toll.note: Starvation and related disease in five northern provinces. Census population loss was 23 million but includes people who migrated.

events.says: Drought-driven crop failure in northern China from 1875, known as the Dingwu Famine, hit Shanxi, Zhili, Henan, Shandong and Shaanxi hardest; heavy rain returned in June 1879.
events.open: The figures are rounded estimates and the range is wide. Provincial counts differ by source, and population-loss figures from censuses mix deaths with migration.

sources.title: Tears from Iron: Cultural Responses to Famine in Nineteenth-Century China

events.name: Indian famines of 1876–1878 and 1896–1902

toll.text: 1876-78: 5.6-9.6 million (careful estimate 8.2). 1896-97: about 1 million officially, 4.5-5 million by later work. 1899-1900: over 1 million, up to 4.5. Roy puts the Deccan famines together at 20-22 million.
toll.note: Low is the 1876-78 floor alone; high is Roy's total for the 1876, 1896 and 1898-99 famines. Official counts covered British-ruled districts only.

events.says: Drought-driven famines under British rule: 1876-78 in Madras, Bombay, Hyderabad and Mysore, later the north, then 1896-97 and 1899-1900 across central, western and northern India.
events.open: Official and demographic estimates differ widely, and totals depend on whether epidemic deaths count. The general article gives 1.25-10 million for 1896-97. Historians debate colonial policy's role.

sources.title: Famines in India: Enduring Lessons (Tirthankar Roy, Economic and Political Weekly 2021)
sources.publisher: London School of Economics (LSE Research Online)

events.name: Russian famine of 1891–1892

toll.text: Some historians attribute no deaths to hunger itself; others give 375,000-400,000, mostly from disease. Robbins put it at about 407,000 and Urlanis at 500,000 for 1892, and Nefedov and Ellman at 1.3 million.
toll.note: Low reflects views that 1892 excess deaths were cholera; the 1.3 million covers the 1889-1893 crisis, not only 1891-92.

events.says: Crop failure after a dry spring and a hard, snowless winter in 1891 struck the Volga region and spread toward the Urals and Black Sea; the state spent heavily on relief and volunteers, including Tolstoy, helped.
events.open: Whether the famine itself caused deaths is disputed. Some attribute 1892's excess deaths to the cholera pandemic; others count 375,000 to 1.3 million as famine victims, depending on method and area.

sources.title: Excess Mortality in Russia in 1868-1912 and Its Historiographic Implications (Nefedov and Ellman)

events.name: Persian famine of 1917–1919

toll.text: Mainstream scholars cited by Wikipedia put deaths from hunger and disease at about 2 million; Mohammad Gholi Majd argues for 8-10 million.
toll.note: Includes cholera, typhus and influenza deaths alongside starvation; the 2 million is a single mainstream figure, not a range.

events.says: During the First World War Iran, though neutral, was occupied by British, Russian and Ottoman forces. Drought, requisitioning and hoarding led to mass hunger, and epidemics followed, in 1917-1919.
events.open: Majd's 8-10 million is not accepted by most academic historians, who call it exaggerated. Majd calls it a genocide; Abrahamian and others reject that label.

sources.title: Imperial wars and the violence of hunger: remembering and forgetting the Great Persian Famine 1917-1919 (Third World Quarterly 45(2), 2024)
sources.publisher: Third World Quarterly / Routledge (record via Tampere University)

sources.title: The Great Famine and Genocide in Persia, 1917-1919 (publisher description of Majd's 8-10 million claim)

events.name: Russian famine of 1921–1922

toll.text: Estimates run from not more than one million up to ten million; an early Soviet figure of about five million is the one most often quoted.
toll.note: Famine plus related disease; no reliable statistics exist, so every figure is an estimate.

events.says: After drought, war and grain requisitioning, a severe famine struck the Volga and Ural regions of Soviet Russia in 1921-1922. Foreign relief, chiefly American, fed millions.
events.open: The toll is unsettled: historians quote about 5 million, with some putting it far lower and others up to 10 million. No reliable death statistics were kept.

sources.title: Book launch: The Big Show in Bololand (Kennan Institute summary of B. Patenaude)

events.name: Soviet famine of 1930–1933 (Holodomor and the Kazakh famine)

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 5.7-8.7 million deaths across the USSR (Davies and Wheatcroft 5.5-6.5 million; Wolowyna 8.7 million), split among Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan.
toll.note: Famine deaths across the whole Soviet Union, not Ukraine alone; excludes lost births. Wikidata carries 5.7 million.

events.says: Forced collectivization and grain procurement caused famine in Ukraine, the North Caucasus, the Volga region, Kazakhstan and elsewhere in the USSR, peaking in 1932-1933.
events.open: Totals and cause are debated. Some scholars call the Ukrainian and Kazakh famines genocides; others, such as Ellman and Wheatcroft, dispute intent. A Kyiv court counted 10 million losses incl. lost births.

sources.title: A Demographic Framework for the 1932-1934 Famine in the Soviet Union (O. Wolowyna, Journal of Genocide Research, 2020)
Oleh Wolowyna on measuring mortality in the Holodomor (report of his all-Union figure of 8.73 million)

events.name: Bengal famine of 1943

toll.text: Wikipedia reports 0.8-3.8 million deaths in Bengal, with Cormac Ó Gráda citing a scholarly consensus near 2.1 million.
toll.note: Starvation plus disease, mainly malaria, aggravated by malnutrition; wartime records were incomplete, especially in rural areas.

events.says: A famine in Bengal and Orissa under British rule in 1943-1944 killed large numbers by starvation and disease during the Second World War, after wartime inflation, lost rice imports and weak relief.
events.open: The toll is uncertain because records were poor. Causes are argued: Amartya Sen stresses lost purchasing power, others stress British wartime policy.

events.name: The Great Chinese Famine

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 15-46 million excess deaths from starvation, with newer estimates concentrated at 30-46 million.
toll.note: Excess deaths; some authors also count overwork or violence. The article's table spans about 3.7 to 55 million.

events.says: A famine in the People's Republic of China from 1959 to 1961, linked to the Great Leap Forward, the commune system, grain procurement and poor weather, caused very high excess mortality.
events.open: The toll is heavily disputed: Wikipedia's table ranges from about 3.7 million (some PRC scholars) to 55 million (Yu Xiguang). Official PRC figures understate the fall in population.

sources.title: China's great famine: 40 years later (V. Smil, BMJ 1999)

events.name: Biafran war and famine

toll.text: Civilian deaths from starvation are put at 500,000 to 2 million by Wikipedia's lead; the ICRC says as many as 3 million died in all, in combat, hunger or sickness.
toll.note: Mostly blockade famine and disease; about 100,000 military deaths are counted separately by Wikipedia. Figures cover the whole war.

events.says: Biafra seceded from Nigeria in 1967 and was surrounded and blockaded by federal forces. The war ended in January 1970, with mass starvation among Biafran civilians.
events.open: Estimates vary with scope. Some scholars, such as Ekwe-Ekwe, call the war a genocide against the Igbo; critics dispute that, though they accept that starvation was used as policy.

sources.title: People on War: Country report Nigeria
sources.publisher: International Committee of the Red Cross

sources.title: Biafra's Secession Triggers Nigerian Civil War (Research Starters)

events.name: Ethiopian famine of 1983–1985

toll.text: Wikipedia reports approximately 300,000 to 1.2 million dead; Africa Watch (Alex de Waal) estimates at least 400,000, not counting resettlement deaths.
toll.note: Famine mortality only; resettlement deaths and war deaths are separate. The widely quoted one million has no scientific basis, per de Waal.

events.says: Drought and war, together with government counter-insurgency and resettlement policy, caused a severe famine in northern Ethiopia in 1983-1985, famously reported by the BBC in 1984.
events.open: The often-quoted UN figure of one million is challenged by de Waal. Human Rights Watch and Oxfam attribute a large share of the deaths to government policy.

sources.title: Evil Days: 30 Years of War and Famine in Ethiopia (Africa Watch report)

events.name: North Korean famine

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 240,000 to 3.5 million deaths from starvation or related illness; a 2011 US Census Bureau study put excess deaths for 1993-2000 at 500,000-600,000.
toll.note: Excess deaths; contemporaneous estimates vary widely and no official count exists.

events.says: A prolonged food shortage in North Korea from the mid-1990s, after the loss of Soviet support, floods and economic failure, caused mass starvation, with deaths peaking in 1997.
events.open: Both extremes of the range are considered unreliable by analysts such as Lankov. Noland calls a 2.5 million figure from a US official almost surely an exaggeration.

sources.title: Famine and Reform in North Korea (M. Noland, Working Paper 03-5)

events.name: Somali famine of 2011

toll.text: The Wikipedia article gives no death figure; a FSNAU/FEWS NET study estimates 258,000 excess deaths in southern and central Somalia, Oct 2010-Apr 2012, within 143,000-273,000.
toll.note: Southern and central Somalia only, Oct 2010 to Apr 2012; about half were children under five. Range is the study's method spread.

events.says: A severe drought in East Africa in 2011-2012 led the UN to declare famine in parts of southern Somalia in July 2011. Many Somalis fled to Kenya and Ethiopia.
events.open: The Wikipedia article for this event states no toll; the range here comes from the FSNAU/FEWS NET study alone. Armed conflict and restricted aid access are said to have worsened the crisis.

sources.title: Mortality among populations of southern and central Somalia affected by severe food insecurity and famine during 2010-2012 (FSNAU and FEWS NET, May 2013; archived copy)

events.name: An Lushan rebellion

toll.text: The 13 to 36 million sometimes quoted comes from comparing census totals before and after, and historians cited here do not treat it as a count of the dead. Cambridge History says hundreds of thousands died in the Central Plain.
toll.note: No agreed figure.

events.says: A civil war in Tang China from 755 to 763, begun by the general An Lushan, in which rebels took the capital Chang'an. It devastated the north and weakened the dynasty.
events.open: Historians including Fitzgerald and Bielenstein reject the census drop as a measure of deaths. A Cambridge economic history says hundreds of thousands perished in the Central Plain.

sources.title: Economic transformation in the Tang-Song transition (755 to 1127), in The Economic History of China
The Reach of the Military: Tang (D. Graff, Journal of Chinese History)

events.name: Siege and massacre at Jerusalem

toll.text: Wikipedia says modern estimates put those killed at between 3,000 and 10,000; medieval chronicles give far higher figures, up to 75,000 or more.
toll.note: Muslims and Jews killed after the city fell; no reliable count exists and the city held roughly 30,000 people.

events.says: Crusaders of the First Crusade besieged Jerusalem from 7 June 1099 and entered on 15 July, then killed many of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
events.open: Numbers in the chronicles are widely seen as inflated. A Cambridge chapter asks whether genocide occurred and concludes it is not necessary to argue that the crusades were genocide.

sources.title: Crusaders and Mass Killing at Jerusalem in 1099 (T. Fudge), in The Cambridge World History of Genocide

events.name: Albigensian Crusade

toll.text: The Wikipedia infobox gives a floor of at least 200,000 Cathars killed over 1209-1229 (citing Tatz and Higgins); neither its prose nor World History Encyclopedia gives a whole-crusade total.
toll.note: A minimum only, no ceiling stated. Béziers (1209) alone: about 10,000 per WHE; the legate's own letter claimed about 20,000, which Strayer thinks too high.

events.says: A military campaign launched by Pope Innocent III against the Cathars of Languedoc in southern France, carried out mainly by northern French forces, with sieges and massacres such as Béziers in 1209.
events.open: No agreed overall toll exists. Some scholars (Lemkin, Pegg, Jonassohn and Björnson) call it genocide; Lerner disputes that, since it targeted a belief, not a people.

events.name: Mongol destruction of Khwarazm and Khorasan
events.wiki: Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire

toll.text: The only overall figure in the Wikipedia article is Steven Ward's 'possibly' 10-15 million, for Mongol violence on the whole Iranian plateau; the article calls chroniclers' city tolls exaggerated.
toll.note: One historian's estimate, wider than 1219-21 and than Khwarazm. Chronicle city counts (e.g. 1.2 million at Gurganj) are judged inflated.

events.says: Genghis Khan's armies invaded the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219-1221, took Bukhara, Samarkand and Gurganj, then devastated Khorasan, including Merv, Nishapur and Herat.
events.open: Medieval chroniclers gave tolls in the hundreds of thousands to millions per city; modern historians treat these as exaggerated, and no accepted total exists.

sources.title: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
Prolegomenon: The Early Period, 615-76/1218-78 (A History of Herat)

events.name: Mongol siege and sack of Baghdad

toll.text: Wikipedia reports Hulegu's own figure of about 200,000 and later Muslim chroniclers' figures of 800,000 to 2 million; the 2024 Medical History article lists 300,000 up to 2 million among the chronicles.
toll.note: Early 1258 sack of Baghdad; may include later deaths among survivors from an epidemic. No count is known.

events.says: A Mongol army under Hulegu besieged Baghdad in early 1258, took it within weeks, looted it, and executed the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim.
events.open: The number killed is unknown. Wikipedia itself gives conflicting Hulegu figures (200,000 or 2 million); chroniclers' numbers grew with retelling, and al-Dhahabi's 300,000 is judged the more realistic.

sources.title: Plague and the Mongol conquest of Baghdad (1258)? A reevaluation of the sources (Brack, Biran, Amitai)
sources.publisher: Medical History (Cambridge University Press), via PubMed Central

events.name: Timur's campaigns

toll.text: The Wikipedia article on Timur gives no overall death toll, only that scholars estimate his campaigns killed millions, plus single events such as about 20,000 at Baghdad (1401).
toll.note: No numeric range in the article; millions is a qualitative statement. Figures for single sieges are chronicle-based.

events.says: Timur, a Turco-Mongol ruler based in Samarkand, conquered Central Asia, Persia, parts of India, Syria and Anatolia between about 1380 and 1405, sacking cities such as Delhi, Aleppo and Baghdad.
events.open: No total is agreed; a Cambridge article warns the Western legend of Timur's cruelty has been embellished beyond plausibility.

sources.title: The Rise of Tīmūr and Western Diplomatic Response, 1390-1405
sources.publisher: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge University Press)

events.name: Spanish conquest and the Taíno of Hispaniola

toll.text: The Wikipedia article gives no total deaths. It gives a pre-contact population of 10,000 to 1,000,000, about 60,000 by 1507 and about 32,000 by 1514, and 80-90% dead within thirty years.
toll.note: Population estimates, not a death count; disease, enslavement and violence are not separated. Library of Congress: about 1 million to 30,000 in 20 years.

events.says: After 1492 the Spanish settlement of Hispaniola brought enslavement, forced labour, famine, massacres such as Jaragua in 1503, and disease, and the Taíno population collapsed within decades.
events.open: The starting population is very uncertain, and scholars differ on how much of the loss was disease versus enslavement and violence; whether it is called genocide is argued. Wikidata lists 8,000 deaths, which fits none of these.

sources.title: Europe Claims America: The Atlantic Joined (1492: An Ongoing Voyage)

events.name: St. Bartholomew's Day massacre

toll.text: Wikipedia gives modern estimates of 5,000 to 30,000 dead across France; World History Encyclopedia gives 5,000 to 25,000. Contemporary Huguenot claims reached 70,000.
toll.note: Covers Paris and the provincial massacres, August to October 1572. No full count was ever compiled; Wikidata lists 10,000 and 30,000.

events.says: From 23-24 August 1572, after the attempt on Admiral Coligny, Huguenot leaders were killed on royal order in Paris, and violence spread to other French cities over following weeks.
events.open: The total is disputed: specialists tend toward lower figures, and bodies thrown in rivers were never counted. Historians also differ on how far the king planned it.

sources.title: The Saint Bartholomew's Massacres in the Provinces

events.name: Thirty Years' War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 4.5 to 8 million military and civilian deaths from battle, famine and disease, of which 1.3 to 1.8 million were military. A Cambridge journal article gives 5 to 8 million.
toll.note: Includes disease and famine deaths. Older claims of up to 12 million are no longer considered realistic. German lands lost roughly 40% of population.

events.says: A war fought mainly in the Holy Roman Empire from 1618 to 1648, beginning as a Bohemian revolt and drawing in most of Europe; the Peace of Westphalia ended it.
events.open: Totals depend on population reconstructions; losses varied sharply by region, and some apparent losses were migration. The range reflects method, not new evidence.

sources.title: Lutheran Religious Life during the Thirty Years War (1618-1648)
sources.publisher: Journal of Ecclesiastical History (Cambridge University Press)

events.name: Cromwellian conquest of Ireland

toll.text: Wikipedia cites one modern estimate of 200,000 killed (137,000 civilians) and William Petty's 1650s figure of over 618,000 dead from the wars since 1641.
toll.note: Petty's figure covers 1641-1653, includes disease, and is thought too high; modern estimates put population loss nearer 15-20%.

events.says: England's Commonwealth army under Oliver Cromwell conquered Ireland from 1649 to 1653, with massacres at Drogheda and Wexford, then a guerrilla war, and land confiscation followed.
events.open: The toll is disputed because Petty's numbers are high and modern ones lower. Whether it was ethnic cleansing or genocide (Coogan) is argued; Wikipedia reports both labels as used by some writers.

sources.title: How many died during Cromwell's campaign?

events.name: Atlantic slave trade and the Middle Passage

toll.text: Deaths on the sea voyage: Wikipedia says up to 2 million of about 12.75 million loaded, and cites Patrick Manning's 1.5 million; the NPS gives about 15% of those carried.
toll.note: Voyage deaths only. Manning separately estimates 4 million died in Africa after capture; those, and deaths after landing, are not included.

events.says: Between roughly 1500 and 1866 about 12 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic into slavery, mostly to Brazil and the Caribbean, and many died on the Middle Passage crossing.
events.open: Voyage-death counts depend on incomplete ship records. Deaths during capture, marches and seasoning are counted differently by different scholars.

events.name: Black War in Tasmania

toll.text: Wikipedia's lead gives 600 to 900 Aboriginal Tasmanians killed, with more than 200 colonists; Clements estimates about 600 and Ryan 838 in the east.
toll.note: Frontier violence 1824-1832. Johnson and McFarlane add 400 or more in the northwest; Clements allows 400 to 1,000.

events.says: A guerrilla conflict between British colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians from the mid-1820s to 1832, including martial law and the 1830 Black Line, that ended with most survivors removed to Flinders Island.
events.open: Death counts differ between historians, and the genocide label is disputed: some say yes, others say the authorities did not intend to destroy the people.

sources.title: Noted works: The Black War
sources.publisher: The Conversation (University of Newcastle historian review)

sources.title: The Black War: The tragic fate of the Tasmanian Aborigines (A History of Tasmania)

events.name: Trail of Tears

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox totals 13,200 to 16,700 deaths across the Cherokee (4,000), Creek and Seminole (3,000), Chickasaw (3,500) and Choctaw (2,500-6,000) removals.
toll.note: About 60,000 people removed 1830-1850. The listed parts add to slightly less than the stated total; NPS says no one knows how many died.

events.says: The US government forcibly moved about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people from the Southeast to Indian Territory after 1830, with many dying of exposure, disease and hunger.
events.open: Counts vary by nation and source. Scholars differ on the label: some call it genocide, others ethnic cleansing, and one historian cited by Wikipedia says it falls short of genocide.

sources.title: The Trail of Tears, 1838-1839 (Little River Canyon National Preserve)

events.name: Taiping Rebellion

toll.text: Wikipedia reports 20-30 million deaths as the most widely cited figure, with some estimates of 73-100 million; Columbia University says more than 20 million. Includes soldiers and civilians, many from famine and plague.
toll.note: No reliable census existed; most deaths are attributed to disease and famine, not battle. All figures are speculative.

events.says: A civil war in Qing China from 1850 to 1864 between the dynasty and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, a rebel state led by Hong Xiuquan that held much of the Yangtze valley and Nanjing.
events.open: The toll is unsettled: the common 20-30 million estimates sit far below others of 73-100 million, and no census exists to settle it.

events.name: Hamidian massacres

toll.text: Wikipedia says historians' figures range from 80,000 to 300,000 Armenians killed in 1894-1896 (the lead gives 100,000 to 300,000); the Armenian National Institute also gives 100,000 to 300,000.
toll.note: Lepsius counted about 88,000 deaths, plus about 100,000 more from famine and disease; the British ambassador said 100,000 by Dec 1895.

events.says: Massacres of Armenians across the Ottoman Empire in the mid-1890s under Sultan Abdul Hamid II, most of them between 1894 and 1896, plus attacks on other Christians such as Assyrians in Diyarbekir.
events.open: Counts differ widely by source. Most scholars do not call these killings part of the 1915 genocide, though some do. Armenian/Western and Ottoman-Turkish accounts frame the events differently.

sources.title: Armenian massacres of the Hamidian period, 1894-1897: an empirical inquiry (J. Verheij, PhD thesis)

events.name: Congo Free State
events.wiki: Atrocities in the Congo Free State

toll.text: Wikipedia gives a population decline of 1.2 to 10 million over 1885-1908; its body also cites a 2020 demographic model of 1 to 5 million. These are population-loss estimates, not counts of killings.
toll.note: Includes disease, famine and falling births as well as violence; no census before 1924, so the 1885 population is itself unknown.

events.says: Under King Leopold II's personal rule, 1885 to 1908, forced rubber collection, violence by the Force Publique and company militias, and epidemics coincided with a steep fall in the Congolese population.
events.open: Estimates range widely; a 2024 Journal of African History note says 1 to 15 million. Most of the decline is attributed to disease. Whether to call it genocide is disputed; many historians say it was not.

sources.title: Atrocities in the Congo Free State
Historical Scholarship and the Public Square: The Belgian Commission on Colonialism Through the Lens of Wiriyamu (Journal of African History 65)

events.name: Herero and Nama genocide

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 40,000 to 80,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama dead in 1904-1908; the range here adds those figures. Cambridge's World History of Genocide puts the total near 75,000.
toll.note: Low and high are sums of the article's two groups. Deaths came from battle, thirst in the Omaheke desert, and camps.

events.says: German colonial forces in South West Africa (now Namibia) crushed the Herero uprising of 1904 and the Nama revolt that followed; many fled into the desert or died in prison camps, 1904 to 1908.
events.open: Counts vary by source (Wikipedia says 40,000-80,000 Herero; a Leiden Journal article gives 65,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama). Germany recognised a genocide in 2015 but denies legal liability for reparations.

sources.title: 'Rivers of Blood and Rivers of Money' (Chapter 26), The Cambridge World History of Genocide
Land, genocide, and kintsugi in Namibia (Leiden Journal of International Law)

events.name: The Armenian genocide

toll.text: Wikipedia says around 1 million Armenians died, with figures from 600,000 to 1.5 million; USHMM says at least 664,000 and possibly as many as 1.2 million. Covers killings, death marches, starvation and disease.
toll.note: Wikidata gives 700,000-1,700,000 (central value 1.2 million); USHMM's range is narrower than the Wikipedia range.

events.says: From 1915 the Ottoman government deported and killed most of the Armenian population of Anatolia, through massacres and marches into the Syrian desert; Armenian communities were largely destroyed by 1917.
events.open: Estimates differ by source. The Republic of Turkey rejects the genocide label; USHMM and most genocide scholars use it. Whether the 1894-96 and 1909 massacres belong to it is also debated.

events.name: Assyrian genocide (Sayfo)

toll.text: No modern count exists. Assyrian delegates claimed 250,000 dead in 1919 and 275,000 in 1923; a Syriac archbishop's figures sum to 180,000. Wikipedia and Gaunt et al. call these unverifiable.
toll.note: Pre-war Assyrian population is itself estimated at 500,000-600,000. Figures are claims made for peace conferences, not demographic counts.

events.says: Ottoman forces and allied Kurdish groups killed and drove out Assyrian/Syriac Christians in southeast Anatolia and Persian Azerbaijan during the First World War, alongside the Armenian genocide.
events.open: The toll is unverified and may be exaggerated or low. Turkey denies a genocide of Assyrians; historian Gaunt calls the term 'Assyrian genocide' anachronistic since Ottomans classed people by religion.

sources.title: Introduction: Contextualizing the Sayfo in the First World War (Gaunt, Atto, Barthoma)

events.name: Greek genocide

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 300,000 to 1,200,000 Ottoman Greeks dead, 1914-1923; its text cites academic estimates from 289,000 to 750,000, and one author's 1.2 million. Some claims run to 1.5 million.
toll.note: A 1921 Greek committee, cited in a Cambridge article, put deaths among deportees at 150,000+. Counts cover very different periods and regions.

events.says: Ottoman and later Turkish nationalist authorities expelled, deported and killed Orthodox Greeks of Anatolia and Pontus between 1914 and 1923; survivors fled to Greece or were exchanged in 1923.
events.open: Toll is unsettled, with Wikidata listing 300,000, 450,000 and 900,000. Turkey rejects the genocide label; the IAGS affirmed it in 2007 by an 83% vote of members voting.

sources.title: Press release: International Genocide Scholars Association officially recognizes Assyrian, Greek genocides (15 Dec 2007)
sources.publisher: International Association of Genocide Scholars (press release issued by Adam Jones, UBC Okanagan)

sources.title: 'This expulsion is explained in many ways': Ottoman Greek Orthodox internal exiles during the Great War (1914-1918)
sources.publisher: Cambridge University Press (New Perspectives on Turkey)

events.name: Great Purge

toll.text: Archives record 681,692 executions in 1937-1938; Wikipedia says scholars estimate 700,000 to 1.2 million deaths, counting executions, camp deaths and deaths soon after release.
toll.note: Low end is the official execution count alone; Wikidata uses the same figure. Older Western estimates of millions are rejected by archival evidence.

events.says: Under Stalin, the NKVD arrested and executed huge numbers of party members, officials, army officers and ordinary people, with mass operations against social and national groups, mainly in 1937 and 1938.
events.open: Totals depend on what is counted (executions, camp deaths, post-release deaths) and on dates. Popular estimates once ran from 500,000 to 7 million, which archives do not support. Wikipedia dates it 1936-1939.

sources.title: Understanding Stalin's Terror against Western Minorities: The National Operations of the NKVD in Contemporary Academic Research (The Historical Journal)

events.name: Nanjing Massacre

toll.text: Wikipedia says newer estimates are 100,000 to 200,000, the Tokyo tribunal found over 200,000, and extremes run from 40,000 (city only) to over 340,000 (wider region). China's official figure is 300,000.
toll.note: Range depends on area (city vs surrounding counties), dates, and whether prisoners of war are counted.

events.says: After taking Nanjing in December 1937, Japanese forces killed large numbers of civilians and prisoners of war and committed mass rape and arson over the following weeks.
events.open: The toll is contested, with Chinese official figures at 300,000 and Japanese scholars mostly giving 100,000-200,000 or lower; Wikipedia notes revisionism on both sides. Wikidata uses 300,000.

sources.title: World War II in the Pacific (Holocaust Encyclopedia)
The Nanjing Massacre: Changing Contours of History and Memory in Japan, China, and the U.S. (Asia-Pacific Journal)

events.name: Babi Yar massacre

toll.text: Wikipedia estimates 100,000 to 150,000 people killed at Babi Yar during the occupation of Kyiv, of whom 33,771 Jews were shot on 29-30 September 1941. USHMM cites Soviet findings of about 100,000.
toll.note: Total covers Jews, Soviet prisoners of war, Roma and others over two years; most bodies were burned in 1943, so no exact count exists.

events.says: A ravine in Kyiv where German forces and collaborators shot tens of thousands, beginning with the Jews of the city on 29-30 September 1941, then Soviet prisoners, Roma and others until 1943.
events.open: The full toll is uncertain because bodies were burned in 1943. The Soviet-era memorial gave about 100,000 without naming the Jewish victims.

sources.title: Mass Shootings at Babyn Yar (Babi Yar) (Holocaust Encyclopedia)

events.name: Siege of Leningrad

toll.text: Wikipedia's lead estimates 1.5 million deaths; its infobox gives 642,000 civilians in the siege plus 400,000 in evacuations, and total dead of 1.3 to 2 million. The National WWII Museum says about 1.5 million.
toll.note: Low end is civilians who died in the city; high end (Glantz) includes soldiers and the wider battle. Figures mix scopes.

events.says: German and Finnish forces besieged Leningrad (now St Petersburg) from September 1941 until January 1944; starvation, cold, shelling and disease killed a large share of the city's population.
events.open: Totals depend on whether soldiers, evacuee deaths and the wider region are counted. Some historians call it genocide; Russia's foreign ministry did in 2024. Others do not use that label.

events.name: Jasenovac concentration camp complex and Ustaša killings

toll.text: Recent scholarship and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum put deaths in the Jasenovac camp complex at roughly 77,000 to 100,000 across 1941-45; the memorial's named list is about 83,000.
toll.note: Camp complex only, not all Ustasa killings in the Independent State of Croatia. Victims were mostly Serbs, with Roma, Jews and others.

events.says: Camps run by the Ustasa regime of the Independent State of Croatia, centred on the village of Jasenovac, held and killed Serbs, Roma, Jews and political opponents from August 1941 to April 1945.
events.open: Postwar Yugoslav figures ran from 500,000 to over a million; some Croatian writers gave 30,000-40,000. Cited sources note records were destroyed and numbers became politicised.

events.name: The Holocaust

toll.text: The Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators murdered about six million Jews in 1941-45; the Wikipedia article gives 5.7 million as a conservative lower figure. Non-Jewish victims are counted separately.
toll.note: Jewish victims only. Millions of other people (Soviet POWs, Poles, Roma and others) killed by Nazi Germany are not in this figure.

events.says: The systematic murder of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, carried out by mass shootings in eastern Europe and by gassing at extermination camps, mainly in occupied Poland.
events.open: The six million is a rounded total built from several kinds of records; lower tallies near 5.7 million exist. Whether non-Jewish victims fall under the term Holocaust varies by author.

sources.title: How Many People did the Nazis Murder? (Holocaust Encyclopedia)

events.name: Bombing of Dresden
events.wiki: Bombing of Dresden in World War II

toll.text: A historians' commission set up by Dresden city council (report 2010) found that between 22,700 and 25,000 people died in the British and US raids of 13-15 February 1945.
toll.note: Residents and refugees together; the city did not separate them. Wartime propaganda and later claims of 200,000 or more are not supported by this work.

events.says: British and American bombers struck Dresden in four raids from 13 to 15 February 1945, causing a firestorm that destroyed much of the city centre in the last months of the war in Europe.
events.open: Whether the bombing was militarily justified or a war crime is still argued. Inflated tolls of 135,000 to 500,000 were spread by Nazi, East German and later far-right sources.

sources.title: Bombing of Dresden in World War II (Wikipedia)

events.name: Firebombing of Tokyo

toll.text: For the night raid of 9-10 March 1945 (Operation Meetinghouse), counts run from the police figure of 83,793 and a scholar's low of 75,000, through about 100,000-110,000, to a scholar's high of 200,000.
toll.note: Covers the 9-10 March raid only. Other Tokyo raids in 1944-45 add further deaths; the whole air campaign on Japan killed over 300,000.

events.says: US B-29 bombers dropped incendiaries on the crowded eastern districts of Tokyo on the night of 9-10 March 1945, burning about 16 square miles and leaving over a million people homeless.
events.open: Japanese and US authorities gave figures near 100,000, which the Wikipedia article says may be low given crowding and wind. Some analysts call the raids a war crime; others do not.

events.name: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.wiki: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

toll.text: Deaths from the two bombs of 6 and 9 August 1945 are put at 150,000-246,000 by Wikipedia (90,000-166,000 Hiroshima, 60,000-80,000 Nagasaki); the Bulletin cites credible tallies as low as 110,000.
toll.note: Deaths within months, civilians and troops. Later cancers excluded; Wikidata's 2013-dated values (286,818; 162,083) are not 1945 tolls.

events.says: The United States dropped one atomic bomb on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and another on Nagasaki on 9 August, in the last days of the Second World War; about half the deaths came on the first day.
events.open: Records were lost and the city populations were uncertain, so early US figures (about 110,000) and later Japanese-led ones (up to about 210,000-246,000) differ. Whether the bombings were justified is debated.

sources.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (Wikipedia)
Counting the dead at Hiroshima and Nagasaki

events.name: Violence of the Partition of India

toll.text: Estimates of deaths in the violence around the 1947 partition of British India run from about 200,000 to 2 million; many scholars settle on roughly one million.
toll.note: Violence only, not the 12-20 million displaced. No census counted these deaths, and no author is cited as explaining how a figure was reached.

events.says: When British India was divided into India and Pakistan in August 1947, Punjab and Bengal were split and millions crossed the new borders amid widespread communal killing.
events.open: The toll is disputed, with the UCLA source giving 500,000-1.5 million and noting few scholars explain their basis. Some writers call the Punjab violence a retributive genocide; others do not.

sources.title: Partition of India
sources.publisher: UCLA Center for India and South Asia

events.name: Indonesian mass killings of 1965–1966

toll.text: The most widely published estimates are at least 500,000 to 1 million killed between October 1965 and March 1966; higher claims reach 2-3 million. Scholars have called 500,000 a consensus figure.
toll.note: Killings of alleged communists and others; imprisonments are separate. Early figures (78,500; 200,000) were set before the killings ended.

events.says: After the failed 30 September 1965 coup attempt, the Indonesian Army and allied militias killed members and suspected sympathisers of the Communist Party and others across the country.
events.open: The total is uncertain; a census-based study says earlier counts rest on anecdote. Some describe the killings as politicide and a few as genocide; Wikipedia says both labels are used.

sources.title: New Findings on the Indonesian Killings of 1965-66 (Journal of Asian Studies)

events.name: Mass killings of the Cultural Revolution

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 1 to 2 million deaths in China's Cultural Revolution (1966-76); Walder's county-record study puts deaths at 1.1 to 1.6 million for 1966-71.
toll.note: Deaths from massacres, factional fighting, suicides and purges; separating them from other causes is hard. Rummel's 7.7 million adds labour-camp deaths.

events.says: Mao Zedong's campaign from 1966 to 1976 to purge supposed capitalist and traditional elements led to Red Guard violence, factional armed clashes, regional massacres and state purges across China.
events.open: Estimates range from hundreds of thousands to several million, depending on what is counted and on state secrecy. Most deaths came in organised campaigns after the mass movements ended.

sources.title: Rebellion and Repression in China, 1966-1971 (Social Science History 38)
sources.publisher: Cambridge University Press (Andrew G. Walder, Stanford)

events.name: 1971 Bangladesh genocide

toll.text: Estimates of Bengali deaths in 1971 range from 26,000 (Pakistan's Hamoodur Rahman Commission) to 3 million (Bangladeshi claims); independent researchers cite 300,000-500,000; a BMJ survey study 125,000-505,000.
toll.note: Mainly civilian Bengali deaths 1971; killings of Biharis (1,000-150,000 by estimate) are separate. Famine and disease deaths are counted differently.

events.says: From 25 March 1971 the Pakistan Army and allied militias carried out a campaign of mass killing, rape and displacement in East Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War, which ended on 16 December.
events.open: The 3 million figure is questioned, and Gerlach (2018) puts total war deaths near half a million. The label genocide is used by Wikipedia and Bangladeshi sources; Gerlach denies a coordinated extermination plan.

sources.title: Fifty years of violent war deaths from Vietnam to Bosnia (BMJ 2008;336:1482)

events.name: Burundian genocide of 1972

toll.text: Conservative estimates of the 1972 Ikiza killings in Burundi are 100,000 to 150,000 dead, with some going to 300,000; Lemarchand gives 200,000-300,000 Hutu, a university bibliography 100,000-200,000.
toll.note: Mostly Hutu killed by the army and government after a Hutu-led uprising. Rebel killings of Tutsi in April are a separate, much smaller count.

events.says: After a Hutu-led rebellion in southern Burundi in April 1972, the Tutsi-dominated army and government killed large numbers of Hutu, especially educated Hutu, over the following months.
events.open: Wikipedia says there is no academic consensus on calling it genocide, selective genocide or ethnic cleansing; some prefer massacre. The government of Burundi suppressed discussion for years.

sources.title: Genocide in Burundi: 1972, an annotated bibliography

events.name: Cambodian genocide

toll.text: Most accepted estimates of excess deaths under the Khmer Rouge (1975-79) are 1.5 to 2 million, about a fifth to a quarter of the population; the Yale program uses roughly 1.7 million.
toll.note: All deaths from Khmer Rouge policy, including execution, starvation, overwork and disease. Civil-war deaths before April 1975 are counted separately.

events.says: From April 1975 to January 1979 the Khmer Rouge regime under Pol Pot emptied the cities, forced people into rural labour and killed or let die an estimated fifth or more of Cambodia's population.
events.open: Figures as low as 1 million and as high as 3 million have been cited; execution is put at 500,000-1.3 million. The 2019 tribunal verdict found genocide against the Vietnamese and the Cham.

events.name: Ethiopian Red Terror

toll.text: Sources range from 10,000 to 980,000 killed in the 1976-78 campaign; a reference work says most experts put it between 10,000 and 150,000.
toll.note: Whole campaign, not just Addis Ababa; no agreed count exists. Wikidata lists 750,000.

events.says: Campaign of arrests and killings by Ethiopia's military government (the Derg) against rival leftist groups, chiefly the EPRP and later MEISON, most intense in Addis Ababa from February 1977.
events.open: The toll is very uncertain (10,000 to 980,000). Ethiopia's courts convicted Mengistu of genocide in absentia in 2006-07; the campaign is also described as political repression.

events.name: Guatemalan genocide

toll.text: The truth commission documented 29,830 killed or disappeared (23,671 executions, 6,159 disappearances) and put all victims of the 1960-96 war at over 200,000.
toll.note: Covers the whole civil war, not only 1981-83; documented count is a floor, 200,000 a wider estimate.

events.says: Army campaign against Maya communities in Guatemala's highlands during the civil war, peaking in 1981-83 with massacres, destroyed villages and forced disappearances.
events.open: The 1999 truth commission found acts of genocide against the Maya. Scholars David Stoll and Carlos Sabino dispute the label and the 200,000 figure, which Stoll calls a very high-end estimate.

sources.title: Truth or Reconciliation Mechanism, 1999 (Guatemala Peace Accord Matrix)
sources.publisher: Kroc Institute, University of Notre Dame

events.name: Rwandan genocide

toll.text: Scholars estimate 500,000-662,000 deaths and Human Rights Watch counted 507,000; the Rwandan government counts 1,074,017 and the UN says more than one million.
toll.note: Government total rests on a pre-war Tutsi population figure that a 2020 scholarly symposium called too high.

events.says: From 7 April to 19 July 1994, Hutu militias and soldiers systematically killed Tutsi, and some moderate Hutu and Twa, across Rwanda after the president's plane was shot down.
events.open: The total is contested: official and UN figures exceed one million, while research-based estimates run roughly 500,000 to 662,000. Wikidata lists 1,000,000.

sources.title: Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda and the United Nations

events.name: Bosnian genocide and the siege of Sarajevo

toll.text: About 8,000 men and boys were killed at Srebrenica; whole-war deaths in 1992-95 are put at about 96,000-97,207 (documentation centre) and 104,732 (ICTY demographers).
toll.note: Low is Srebrenica only; high is all war deaths on every side, not genocide victims alone. About 10,500 remain missing.

events.says: Ethnic cleansing of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats by Bosnian Serb forces during the 1992-95 war, including the July 1995 Srebrenica killings and expulsions.
events.open: Courts found genocide at Srebrenica; whether the wider campaign counts depends on the definition used. Denial persists. War-wide totals differ by database. Wikidata's 8,372 is Srebrenica only.

events.name: Congo wars

toll.text: The International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million excess deaths from August 1998 to April 2007; Simon Fraser University's HSRP argued the figure should be about 860,000.
toll.note: Excess deaths from all causes, mostly disease and hunger, and running four years past the 2003 end; the 1996-97 war is not counted.

events.says: Congo's wars from 1996: the Rwanda- and Uganda-backed overthrow of Mobutu, then the 1998-2003 war that drew in nine African states and about 25 armed groups, fought mainly in the east.
events.open: The IRC and HSRP disagree on method and baseline death rates; HSRP says earlier IRC surveys were flawed and many would have died anyway. IRC authors defend their estimate.

sources.title: Mortality in the Democratic Republic of Congo: An ongoing crisis

events.name: Darfur genocide

toll.text: Estimates run from 100,000 to 400,000 (a 2015 range), with 200,000 for 2003-05 and about 300,000 for 2003-08; a Lancet study gave 298,271 excess deaths (CI 178,258-461,520).
toll.note: Excess deaths include disease and displacement, not only killing; the upper bound is the top of a statistical interval.

events.says: Killing and displacement of Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa civilians in Darfur, Sudan, by government forces and Janjaweed militia from 2003, with burned villages and widespread rape.
events.open: Sudan's government called a 300,000 UN estimate grossly inflated. The ICC has charged genocide in individual cases; the Wikipedia article covers 2003-05 while this event runs to 2010.

sources.title: Patterns of mortality rates in Darfur conflict (Degomme and Guha-Sapir, The Lancet, 2010)

events.name: Yazidi genocide

toll.text: The UN was reported as saying about 5,000 Yazidis were killed; a 2017 PLOS Medicine survey estimated 3,100 killed (95% CI 2,100-4,400) in the August 2014 attack.
toll.note: Survey covers the few days of August 2014 and counts deaths on Mount Sinjar from thirst and hunger as well as executions.

events.says: Islamic State attack on the Yazidis of Sinjar, northern Iraq, from August 2014: killing of men, abduction and enslavement of women and children, and forced conversion, continuing to 2017.
events.open: Early figures near 5,000 killed were lowered by the survey to 2,100-4,400, while estimated abductions (4,200-10,800) were higher. A UN Human Rights Council report found ISIS committed ongoing genocide.

sources.title: Mortality and kidnapping estimates for the Yazidi population in the area of Mount Sinjar, Iraq, in August 2014 (Cetorelli et al.)

events.name: Rohingya genocide

toll.text: MSF surveys estimated at least 6,700 Rohingya killed from 25 August to 24 September 2017; a 2018 household-survey study estimated at least 24,000-25,000 killed since August 2017.
toll.note: Low bound covers one month; both figures are extrapolated from refugee surveys in Bangladesh. Wikidata has no figure.

events.says: Myanmar military operations against Rohingya Muslims in Rakhine State, in late 2016 and from August 2017, with killings, village burnings and flight of over 700,000 people to Bangladesh.
events.open: Myanmar's government dismissed UN findings as exaggerated. UN agencies, ICC officials and rights groups have called it genocide; several countries call it ethnic cleansing.

sources.title: Myanmar/Bangladesh: MSF surveys estimate that at least 6,700 Rohingya were killed during the attacks in Myanmar

events.name: Syrian civil war

toll.text: The UN rights office estimated 306,887 civilians killed from March 2011 to March 2021; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported about 656,493 total deaths by March 2025.
toll.note: Low is civilians only, direct deaths, to 2021; high is all deaths to 2025 from one monitor. Wikidata lists 570,000.

events.says: Armed conflict from March 2011, when protests against Bashar al-Assad were met with force, involving government, rebel, Kurdish-led, jihadist and foreign forces until Assad fell in December 2024.
events.open: No agreed total: UN figures are minimum verified counts to 2021, the UN Commission of Inquiry gave over 580,000 by May 2021, and monitors count differently and later.

sources.title: Syria: Decade of brutal war left nearly 307,000 civilians dead
